problemStatement.formal:
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be an infinite set for which there exists some $\epsilon>0$ such that in any subset of $A$ of size $n$ there are always at least $\epsilon n$ with no three on a line.

Is it true that $A$ is the union of a finite number of sets where no three are on a line?



A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il, and R\"{o}dl.

See also [774] and [847].

builtItems: Confirmed AreCollinear, NonTrilinear, IsEpsNonTrilinear, and IsWeaklyNonTrilinear are the core definitions.
Confirmed empty/singleton/pair nontrilinear facts, epsilon monotonicity, pigeonhole, finite weak nontrilinearity, and finite case theorems are proved.
Confirmed ErdosProblem846 is the only axiom and ErdosProblem846_contrapositive is theorem-backed.
insights: The infinite finite-union conclusion is not proved; it is represented by the ErdosProblem846 axiom.
Finite point sets are handled theorematically, so the open content is genuinely infinite/combinatorial.
The formal geometry is intentionally lightweight: collinearity is an affine-dependence existential over R.
